# Projected Housing Needs {#sec-projections} ## How many more people: population to 2050 Fauquier is undoubtedly growing, even when its growth has been stable since 2000. Fauquier's population is projected to grow from 74,577 residents in 2024[^base-pop] to 93,171 by 2050, an increase of about 18,594 residents. This 24.9% increase in population drives every downstream housing-need estimate in this chapter. [^base-pop]: The base population is the ACS 2020–2024 5-year estimate, which runs modestly below the PEP July-2024 point-in-time estimate (~75,865) used in @sec-demographics; see @sec-data-notes for the reconciliation. ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Fauquier is projected to reach about 93,000 residents by 2050](projections_files/figure-html/fig-pop-projection-1.png){#fig-pop-projection fig-align='left' fig-alt='Column charts of projected population for 2030, 2040, and 2050, shown in two panels. The Fauquier County panel rises from about 77,600 in 2030 to 84,800 in 2040 to 93,200 in 2050. The Warrenton panel rises from about 10,700 to 11,700 to 12,800 over the same years. Both grow steadily; the county adds far more people in absolute terms.' width=100%} ::: ::: Growth is steady across each decade, from 77,588 in 2030 to 93,171 in 2050. This is a 20.1% gain over twenty years, outpacing Virginia's projected 14.2% statewide growth until 2050. Warrenton is projected to grow in parallel, from 10,693 residents in 2030 to 12,841 in 2050: up 2,148 residents (also a 20.1% increase). ::: {.callout-warning} ## Data note: Bealeton Bealeton has no separate Weldon Cooper projection and is carried through the county totals. ::: ## How many more households Using the average-household-size method, or the number of occupied housing units multiplied by the average household size, the county grows from 26,720 households in 2024 to 33,515 by 2050. This is about 6,795 net new households or a 25.4% increase in households. ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The county is projected to add roughly 6,800 households by 2050](projections_files/figure-html/fig-hh-projection-1.png){#fig-hh-projection fig-align='left' fig-alt='Line chart of projected total households in Fauquier County from a 2024 base of about 26,700 to 2050. The lead average-household-size series rises to about 33,515 by 2050, an increase of roughly 6,800 households. A faint dashed constant-headship reference line tracks just below it, ending at about 33,382. The two methods nearly coincide.' width=100%} ::: ::: Compared with constant-headship sensitivity, which measures projected population outcomes based on the proportion of people in a given demographic group that are a head of household, average household size nearly coincides with an estimate of 33,382 households by 2050 (or 6,662 additional households). Only using headship could over or under estimate the projected growth, because of an increase in young adult headship or conversely more multigenerational families. ::: {.callout-warning} ## Data note: choice of method This is a difference of only about 133 households, so the choice of method does not materially change the total. This 6,795 increased figure is the denominator for the production need (@fig-production-need) and the tenure-by-income allocation (@tbl-needs-allocation) that follow. ::: ## Can production keep pace? Based on these estimates, the county needs about 269 new units per year to house the projected growth by 2050, plus at least a 3% vacancy allowance. On the numbers alone, the county's recent production roughly keeps pace with projected need, essentially level with the 266 units per year the county permitted over 2020–2025. The baseline need is lighter in upcoming years, with only about 204 units/year required through 2030, rising toward the recent pace as growth compounds. The build pressure, or need to add units, is in near-term and more specific to the type and price of what is built, not the overall raw count. This inverts the Greater Piedmont REALTOR's study's finding that units needed (307/yr) exceeds the current building pace. The difference in calculations is relative to the household-size assumptions made. This study uses the county's actual 2020–2024 ACS average household size of 2.78, whereas the GP study's +7,737-household figure back-implies a roughly 2.7-person household. ::: {.callout-warning} ## Why household size matters A larger average person size spreads the same population over fewer new households, ultimately lowering the annual unit need; the full reconciliation is documented in the Data & Methodology appendix (@sec-data-notes). ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Recent building has roughly kept pace with projected household growth](projections_files/figure-html/fig-production-need-1.png){#fig-production-need fig-align='left' fig-alt='Column chart of the annualized new housing units needed to house projected household growth in Fauquier County, over three horizons: about 204 per year through 2030, 244 per year through 2040, and 269 per year through 2050 on the average-household-size method. A dashed horizontal reference line marks the 2020–2025 building-permit pace of about 266 units per year. The 2050-horizon need sits just above that line; earlier horizons sit below it.' width=100%} ::: ::: Keeping pace with the baseline count is admirable but not the same as meeting need, though. The affordability gaps (@fig-rental-gap, @fig-ownership-gap) and interviews show the recent product mix has skewed towards the top of the market. The forward challenge is in composition that can meet the diverse needs of those described in @tbl-needs-allocation. ## How much does the answer swing? One assumption sets the range The estimate for the baseline need for units is only as firm as its household-size assumption. Holding the county's actual 2.78-person household size average constant yields about 269 units needed per year, whereas letting size drift down to 2.60 people per household pushes the baseline units needed to 361 units. Therefore, a plausible reading of the same population projection spans roughly 269–361 units per year. ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Household-size assumptions put annual need between 270 and 360 units](projections_files/figure-html/fig-need-range-1.png){#fig-need-range fig-align='left' fig-alt='Column chart of the annual new-housing-units needed through 2050 under three average-household-size assumptions, holding the projected 2050 population fixed at 93,171. If household size holds at 2.78 (the county\'s actual current average), need is about 269 units per year. If it declines modestly to 2.70, need rises to about 309. If it continues down to 2.60, need reaches about 361. A dashed reference line marks the 2020–2025 building-permit pace of 266 per year, essentially level with the size-holds scenario. The Greater Piedmont regional study\'s estimate of 307 per year falls between the first two bars, inside the band.' width=100%} ::: ::: 269 units per year is a conservative floor of that estimate range, not its midpoint, sitting essentially on the 2020–2025 permit pace of 266 units/yr.[^gp-range] The floor is the locally-grounded case: Fauquier's own household size has not fallen, measuring about 2.76 in 2010 and 2.76 in 2020 (decennial), and 2.78 in 2024 (ACS). This household size is flat-to-rising, bucking the national downward drift. The 361/yr high end of this estimate range, therefore, is not an extrapolation of local history. It is a sensitivity that assumes the county begins converging toward the smaller households as otherwise seen statewide (Virginia averages 2.52). [^gp-range]: The Greater Piedmont study's 307 units/yr estimate falls inside the range, back-implying about a 2.7-person household. ## From new arrivals to full need: a scope ladder How widely "need" is defined changes the units needed. Policy is what can ensure housing unit types developed meet the needs of Fauquier's new arrivals. Read strictly, the county needs 6,795 units to house projected household growth or about 261/yr. Adding a 3% vacancy allowance lifts that to 6,999 or 269/yr until 2050. Layering in today's affordability backlog adds roughly 3,598 units that are needed. This is calculated with a data-grounded 1,059-unit rental deficit estimated for below 80% AMI households (@fig-rental-gap), plus a conservative, assumption-driven estimate for 2,539 ownership units. The estimated ownership share needed is about one-third of the 7,616 units estimated for the sub-80%-AMI ownership shortfall (the raw for-sale snapshot is not a build target). Adding in these estimates raises the need to 10,597 units built or 408/yr. ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The 'units needed' total depends on how widely you define need](projections_files/figure-html/fig-scope-ladder-1.png){#fig-scope-ladder fig-align='left' fig-alt='Stacked column chart showing cumulative housing units needed through 2050 as the definition of need widens across four steps. Step 1, housing new household growth alone, is about 6,795 units. Step 2 adds a 3% vacancy allowance for about 6,999. Step 3 adds the existing affordability backlog — a data-grounded rental deficit of about 1,059 units plus an assumed ownership component of about 2,539 — reaching about 10,597. Step 4 adds replacement of aging, obsolete stock at an assumed 0.25% per year, about 1,860 units, for a total near 12,457. Each added segment is a distinct color; the ownership-backlog and replacement segments are labeled as assumption-driven.' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ## Reading the ladder The two rightmost rungs are determined partly on stated assumptions and should be read as scope, not precision. ::: The county's stock is aging — median year built 1987, with about 56% built before 1990, so some replacement demand is real even though its size is assumed. To replace obsolete stock involves an assumption since permits capture additions, but not demolitions. At a conservative 0.25%/yr of the 28,621-unit stock, adds about 1,860 units in replaced/updated housing stock. Altogether, the full-scope total comes near 12,457 units or 479/yr to add supply, add additional under 80% AMI units, and replace low quality/ high maintenance stock. The single "units needed" number is a definitional choice, not a fact. Housing only new arrivals points to needing about 269/yr. Also clearing the existing shortfall for lower income households - the vast majority of the county - and replacing obsolete stock roughly doubles that. Critically, the headline ~7,000-unit need already approaches — and the full-scope 12,457 far exceeds — the county's existing by-right service-district build-out capacity; see @sec-conclusions for the policy implications. ## An aging county: the 65+ surge The 65-and-older population climbs from 17,157 in 2030 to 18,246 in 2040, then holds essentially flat at 18,208 in 2050, as the leading edge of the baby-boom cohort ages through. The surge is concentrated in the next 15 years. ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The senior population surges through 2040, then plateaus near 18,200](projections_files/figure-html/fig-senior-projection-1.png){#fig-senior-projection fig-align='left' fig-alt='Line chart of projected senior population in Fauquier County for 2030, 2040, and 2050. The 65-and-older line rises from about 17,200 in 2030 to 18,200 in 2040 and holds near 18,200 in 2050. The 75-and-older line rises more steeply from about 7,400 to 9,900 and holds near 9,800 — so the older, higher-need group grows fastest and becomes a larger share of all seniors.' width=100%} ::: ::: The 75-and-older group grows faster and deeper, from 7,371 to 9,939 before easing to 9,844. The higher-need and older-senior share of all seniors rises from about 43% to 54% over the next 20 years. This is the forward-looking counterpart to the current-state senior profile in @sec-populations (65+ already 17% of residents, most owning their homes). The demand signal is for accessible, lower-maintenance, and smaller units, where aging-in-place options and downsizing product in the current stock largely lacks. ## Where the need lands: tenure and income Following the county's current tenure and income mix, the projected 6,795 new households are split roughly between 5,267 owners (78%) to 1,528 renters (22%). The single largest block is owner households above 100% AMI or 3,566 units - who are likely already served by current permitting and development plans. ::: {#tbl-needs-allocation .cell layout-align="left" tbl-cap='Projected need spans every income band — but the existing gap is deepest at the bottom'} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

In the lowest owner and renter income bands, the current affordable-unit deficit (from @sec-gaps) dwarfs the projected new need. Even building for all projected growth would leave the existing shortfall for under 80% AMI households untouched. Because the allocation holds today's income distribution constant, it describes where demand will arise, not where it is affordable. Read alongside the current gaps (@fig-rental-gap, @fig-ownership-gap), it frames the forward task as delivering units at price points the recent market (@sec-market-ownership) has not. For those that said, "Aging in place and downsizing seniors and returning young people have no options," the county must add about 269 units per year to keep pace with household formation. By addressing seniors' needs, with accessible and low maintenance housing options, young folks returning will be competing for the same units. Without addressing this gap in options across the household spectrum, the supply in the county will continue to increase but only widens the housing and affordability gap. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Town spotlight — Warrenton grows with the county; Bealeton is folded into the county total Weldon Cooper projects the **Town of Warrenton to grow from 10,693 residents in 2030 to 12,841 by 2050** (+2,148, 20.1%), a pace close to the county's own 20.1% over 2030–2050 (@fig-pop-projection). As a major water-and-sewer service area within the county's eight service districts, Warrenton is where much of the projected household growth can physically be absorbed. **Bealeton is not projected separately** — Weldon Cooper publishes totals only for counties and large incorporated towns, and Bealeton is an unincorporated census-designated place — so its share of growth is carried inside the Fauquier County totals throughout this chapter. :::
